title: Line, bar, scatter, histogram, box
summary: Five chart types and the question each one answers.

steps.title: Line and bar
body: - A **line chart** shows how a value changes over an ordered axis, usually time. The line implies continuity
- A **bar chart** compares a value across categories. Bars start at zero, so their *length* is the value.
ax.barh(names, values)                       # horizontal: good for long labels
Do not join categories with a line: there is nothing "between" North and South.

steps.title: A bar chart
prompt: Write `plot_totals(totals)` where `totals` is a dict `{category: value}`. Draw a vertical bar chart with one
bar per category in dict order, set the title `Revenue by region` and the y label `Revenue`, and return `(fig, ax)`.
steps.starter:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def plot_totals(totals):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.plot(list(totals), list(totals.values()))
    return fig, ax
hints: Categories are not a trend: use `ax.bar(names, values)` instead of `ax.plot`.
template: Dojo.eq("bar heights", [40.0, 6.0, 36.0], [float(p.get_height()) for p in dojo_ax.patches])

steps.title: Histograms
body: A **histogram** shows the *distribution* of one numeric variable: it cuts the range into bins and draws a bar
for how many values fall in each.
It answers "what values are typical, how spread out are they, is there a long tail?". The bin count changes the
picture: too few hides shape, too many turns into noise. Try a few.

steps.explain: Four bins, so four bars. Bins include their left edge; the last bin also includes its right edge, so 8 lands in [6, 8].

steps.title: Distribution of order values
prompt: Write `plot_distribution(values, bins)` that draws a histogram of `values` with `bins` bins, titled
`Order values`, x label `Value`, y label `Orders`, and returns `(fig, ax)`.
template: Dojo.eq("every value counted", 200, int(sum(p.get_height() for p in dojo_ax.patches)))

steps.title: Scatter and box plots
body: - A **scatter plot** shows the relationship between two numeric variables, one dot per observation:
`ax.scatter(area, price)`. Look for direction, strength, curves and outliers.
- A **box plot** summarises a distribution in five numbers (median, quartiles, whiskers) plus outliers, and is
ideal for comparing several groups side by side: `ax.boxplot([north, south], tick_labels=["North", "South"])`.
A histogram shows one distribution in detail; box plots compare many distributions compactly.

steps.prompt: Match each question to the chart that answers it.
pairs: How did weekly visitors change this year?
Which store sold the most last month?
What do typical delivery times look like?
Do bigger houses sell for more?
How do delivery times differ between three couriers?

steps.title: Size against price
prompt: Write `plot_relationship(df)` where `df` has columns `area` and `price`. Draw a scatter plot with `area` on the
x axis and `price` on the y axis, label the axes `Area (m²)` and `Price`, title it `Price vs area`, and return `(fig, ax)`.
template: Dojo.eq("one dot per row", 4, len(dojo_ax.collections[0].get_offsets()) if dojo_ax.collections else 0)
Dojo.eq("x is area", [50.0, 70.0, 90.0, 120.0], [float(x) for x, y in dojo_ax.collections[0].get_offsets()] if dojo_ax.collections else [])
